route/rm: Teaching a model from people's picks has so far taken two trainings. First, fit a reward model to the preference pairs.
route/loop: Then, in a loop, sample an answer, score it, subtract the K L penalty, Kullback and Leibler's charge for drifting from the reference, and take a policy gradient step.
route/cost: That is a lot of machinery: a second model to train, and a loop that keeps sampling and scoring new answers.
route/dpo: In twenty twenty three, Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell and colleagues at Stanford cut out the middle. Their method trains on the pairs directly: direct preference optimization, D P O.
route/title: Their paper's title says how: your language model is secretly a reward model.
settle/charge: Start from the K L penalty's charge for one answer: beta times its log-ratio, summed over its tokens. The more the model favors an answer over the reference, the more it pays.
settle/two: Take two answers to one prompt. The reference gives each a half. The reward is two for the first answer and one for the second, and beta is one.
settle/shift: Train on reward minus charge. The model shifts toward the first answer, which pays more, and as it does, that answer's charge rises.
settle/level: It stops when reward minus charge is the same for both answers: if one still paid more, moving probability to it would gain.
settle/nums: Here, that happens at about zero point seven three and zero point two seven. The charges are about zero point three eight, and minus zero point six two.
settle/net: For the first answer, reward minus charge is two minus zero point three eight: one point six two.
settle/net2: For the second, it is one plus zero point six two: one point six two again. Level.
settle/flip: Turn that around. Each reward is its answer's charge, plus one number shared by both answers.
settle/gap: And a shared number is what a pick never sees: as with the reward model, only the gap matters. The charges are one apart, just as the rewards are.
settle/secret: So, as far as any pick can tell, beta times the log-ratio is the reward. That is the secret in the title.
settle/rhat: It is called the implicit reward, r hat: the hat marks a reward that is implied, with no reward model behind it.
pairs/back: D P O runs this backwards. It never trains a reward model: it trains the model until its own implicit reward predicts the labelers' picks.
pairs/lp: First, one answer. A whole answer's log-probability is its tokens', added up. Say the model gives an answer a log-probability of minus twelve, and the reference, minus fifteen.
pairs/imp: The log-ratio is the difference: three. With beta at zero point one, the implicit reward is zero point three.
pairs/pair: Now a pair: the chosen answer, y w, w for winner, and the rejected one, y l, l for loser. Their log-ratios are three and minus one.
pairs/loss: Put their implicit rewards into the reward model's loss: minus ln sigma of the winner's reward minus the loser's.
pairs/m: The log-ratios are four apart, and beta times that gap, zero point four, is called the margin: how far the chosen answer leads.
pairs/val: Sigma of zero point four is about zero point six, and minus its log is about zero point five one.
moves/step: Each step that lowers the loss widens the margin: the chosen answer grows more likely, relative to the reference, and the rejected one less likely.
moves/ref: The reference never moves. It is frozen, and every log-ratio is measured against it.
moves/wrong: As with the reward model, the push is biggest on pairs the model ranks the wrong way round.
moves/needs: So all it needs is the pairs, the model being trained, and a frozen reference: no reward model, and no sampling.
